...and end up in the dumpster, a landfill, or repurposed into something else entirely.
Your metaphor captures a harsh, cynical view of human worth, but it perfectly mirrors a documented psychological phenomenon known as prototype theory and appearance bias. Interestingly, academic researchers have studied this exact crossover between how we judge human looks and how we judge grocery store items.
The Psychology of the "Perfect Prototype"
In cognitive science, our brains rely on an idealized prototype—a mental blueprint of what a specific object "should" look like. 
ScienceDirect.com
The Supermarket Standard: Mainstream grocery chains train consumers to expect perfectly symmetrical, vibrant fruits and vegetables. Anything knobby, multi-legged, or discolored is filtered out by suppliers before it ever reaches the shelf. 
www.braunhousehold.com
 +1
The Human Crossover: A study by Columbia Business School titled "From People to Produce" found a direct link between how people judge humans and how they judge food. The researchers discovered that individuals who strongly believe a person's outward appearance reflects their inner character or personality are the exact same people who aggressively reject "ugly" produce. 
Columbia Business School
 +1
Where the "Failed Prototypes" Actually Go
While your prompt suggests they just get thrown away, the global food system (and human society) has had to find creative ways to handle things that don't fit the standard mold:
Destination	What Happens to the "Imperfect" Item
The Discount Box	Retailers market them under self-deprecating labels like "Ugly But Delicious" or "Imperfect" to appeal to bargain hunters.
Specialty Channels	Services like Misfits Market or pop-up concepts like Utrecht's Crooked Supermarket intentionally curate these exact "failed prototypes" for consumers who value substance over symmetry.
Processing & Pureeing	Deformed produce is often chopped up, juiced, or pureed. Once a knobby carrot is blended into a soup or a bruised apple is turned into sauce, its lack of an "aesthetically pleasing look" becomes completely irrelevant.
Ultimately, whether dealing with produce or people, the bias toward an "idealized prototype" often causes society to discard or overlook immense value simply because it isn't packaged in a standard, symmetrical box.

Killing your darlings is the ultimate test of a creator. As a creative technologist, you know firsthand that some of the most complex code, clever features, or ambitious concepts simply don't fit the final user experience. 
When a prototype doesn't serve the core purpose, the cleanest move is to cut the sentimentality and throw it in the bin to clear space for what actually works.
